summary:
The defining event of early November 2026 was the November 3 election, in which voters in ten states decided 41 local data center ballot measures and favored restrictions in 40 of them. Ohio was the epicenter with 21 measures: voters enacted full or 25 MW-threshold bans in Trenton, Piqua, Hubbard, Sunbury, Conneaut, Defiance, Granville, Oregon, Pataskala, Upper Sandusky and Urbana, overturned roughly 550 acres of data center rezonings in Wilmington, and approved new oversight requirements in Grove City and Perry Village. Trenton's Issue 17 — passed with roughly 80% support — blocks the annexation path for a planned 1,000 MW Amazon campus, one of the clearest instances yet of a ballot measure stopping a specific hyperscale project. Kansas voters enacted bans in El Dorado, Emporia and Ottawa; Maine towns approved a ban and three moratoriums; Alhambra became the first California city to ban data centers by popular vote; and Edgewater, Florida wrote its council-enacted ban into the city charter. The lone pro-development result among the 41 measures came in Harwood, North Dakota.
The election also reshaped the statewide picture in Texas, where Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has pledged to keep data center approvals paused until the Legislature passes ratepayer and water protections when it convenes in January 2027 — signaling that the permitting freeze Governor Abbott imposed through grid and environmental agencies will likely persist or expand through the transition. Texas and New York remain the only states with statewide pauses in force: New York's Executive Order 62 hyperscale moratorium continues while the broader Responsible Data Center Development Act sits unsigned on Governor Hochul's desk, with New York City's mayor now publicly urging her to sign it. In Florida, the Public Service Commission rejected Duke Energy Florida's proposed large-load tariff in the first contested test of SB 484, finding it failed to guarantee that every large customer would cover its full cost of service — an early sign that ratepayer-protection statutes will be enforced strictly.
Below the state level, the moratorium wave continued unabated. Councils and boards adopted new pauses or bans in Scarborough and Westbrook, Maine (both permanent bans replacing earlier moratoriums), Mooresville, North Carolina, the City of Newberry, South Carolina, Hamburg, New York, and Caledonia, Minnesota, while West Richland, Washington confined data centers to light-industrial zones. Not every community is restricting: Hermantown, Minnesota approved a Google data center over heavy public opposition, Louisville cleared a 1.64 million-square-foot hyperscale campus, and Spartanburg County, South Carolina advanced negotiated development agreements worth billions even while its moratorium holds. Trends to watch: whether Ohio's voter-enacted bans trigger the legal challenges developers have threatened elsewhere; the December ERCOT grid audit deadline and the January Texas legislative session; Loudoun County, Virginia's November 17 vote on pausing application decisions in the nation's largest data center market; and whether the near-uniform success of restriction measures on November 3 accelerates copycat ballot initiatives in 2027.
